quick.h1: Health funding is concentrated in immunization, TB, primary care and maternal and child health; NCDs and institution-building (workforce, medicines) are the next focus
msgs: Agreement reached with the World Bank on additional financing for primary care (USD 15 million) (11/5). It tops up the existing primary care programme and is expected to continue beyond 2027.
On NCDs, national policy is ahead and funding is lagging.
Following "Healthy Heart" and the chronic kidney disease programme, a draft NCD Strategy 2027–2032 is under discussion (11/6). NCD projects are small.
A new funding source for hospital modernization.
The Islamic Development Bank is discussing the modernization of 3 hospitals with 850 beds (10/28–11/3), alongside Japan's equipment cooperation (southern regional core hospitals, JPY 430 million).
Germany's sector support and maternal and child health programme, and the Global Fund's TB and HIV grants, among others, expire in December 2026. Succession is next year's focus.

Mental health (68 psychiatrists nationwide), medicines (Essential Medicines List approved in October), emergency care and primary care quality. Institutions are moving, but there are no donor projects.

themes: National policy (heart, kidney, cancer, draft NCD strategy) and regulation (ban on energy drinks) are advancing together. Projects are small, leaving ample room for donors.
Withdrawal of medical school accreditation, a change in the licensing authority and digital training continue the institutional overhaul. Support is limited to the Swiss medical education reform.

sections.h: Health status and health system overview
sections.msg: Life expectancy and child mortality have improved, but financing and the health workforce remain the weakest in the European Region.

paras.t: Life expectancy rose from 70.7 years (2015) to 72.4 years (2024). National statistics put it at 72.0 years in 2023 (68 for men, 77 for women).
paras.b: Life expectancy 70.7 years (2015) → 72.4 years (2024)

paras.t: Infant mortality fell from 15.2 per 1,000 live births (2021) to 13.1 (2024), and maternal mortality, according to Ministry of Health figures, fell from 37.1 to 25.7 per 100,000 live births.
paras.b: Infant mortality 15.2 → 13.1; maternal mortality (MoH) 37.1 → 25.7

paras.t: Health spending was 5.4% of GDP (2021), well below 8.5% in 2012. At USD 302 per capita (PPP), it is the lowest in the WHO European Region. Health accounted for 8.6% of government expenditure (2021).
paras.b: Health spending 5.4% of GDP, USD 302 per capita: lowest level in the European Region

paras.t: Out-of-pocket payments accounted for 40.7% of health spending (2021). In 2014, about 13% of households incurred catastrophic health spending that strained household budgets.

There are 215 physicians (2021) and 407 nurses (2020) per 100,000 population, among the lowest levels in the European Region. Primary care has about 3,000 vacant physician posts. The number of hospitals fell from 450 (1997) to 135 (2020).
paras.b: 215 physicians per 100,000; about 3,000 vacant PHC physician posts

paras.t: The National Development Programme 2030 notes that 40% of households face constraints in accessing health services and medicines, and identifies "outflow of personnel and shortage of specialists" and "lack of an integrated approach to digitalization" as challenges.

Progress has come through disease-specific programmes (immunization, maternal and child health, TB), while weak health system foundations (financing and workforce) are now the barrier to further gains.
paras.b: Gains came from disease programmes; foundations (financing, workforce) are the next barrier

paras.t: Background: financing, workforce and regional disparities

According to the WHO European Observatory, the out-of-pocket share of health spending fell from 57.2% (2016) to 40.7% (2021). Per capita, public spending was USD 161 and out-of-pocket spending USD 123 (PPP), and public health expenditure was 2.9% of GDP (2021). In 2019, health spending comprised inpatient care 31.9%, medicines 30.1% and outpatient care 26.1%.

On the workforce, physicians per 100,000 fell from 226 (2013) to 215 (2021), and nurses from 558 (2013) to 407 (2020). Only 30% of young doctors who complete training enter the public health system; the report cites harsh working conditions and punitive treatment. Family doctors make up 12% of all physicians (2021), and more than half are at retirement age, with the share higher in rural areas: 73% in Naryn Region and 75% in Issyk-Kul Region.

Regional disparities are wide: some rural areas have about 70 physicians per 100,000 (one per 1,429 people), against 225 in Bishkek and 246 in Osh. Advanced care is available only in Bishkek. Internal migrants (about 18% of the population) often cannot enrol in mandatory health insurance because they lack documents.
Labour migration abroad is substantial, with remittances equal to 25–30% of GDP, mostly from Russia. The report acknowledges emigration of health workers but notes that data on it are scarce.

With fewer physicians, an ageing family-doctor workforce and young doctors not entering the public system, the primary care workforce is thinning, starting in rural areas. Combined with low public spending (2.9% of GDP), weaknesses in workforce and financing are reinforcing each other.

sections.msg: Health policy is organized in three tiers: NDP 2030 Section 9.4 → Health Programme 2019–2030 → disease-specific national programmes.

fig.cap: Figure 1-2 Policy architecture (status as of November 2026)
levels: National Development Programme 2030, Section 9.4 "Accessible and Sustainable Health Care"

6 targets and 5 challenges (85% health insurance coverage, life expectancy 75, maternal mortality 22, under-5 mortality 14.0, 30% reduction in premature NCD mortality, 70% coverage of prevention and primary care)
10 priority areas, grouped on this site into 3 pillars: (1) primary care and public health, (2) hospitals and emergency care, (3) health system foundations
14 plans and regulations: 8 in force, 3 drafts, 1 nearing expiry, 2 areas with no stand-alone plan (Table 1-1)

paras.t: Overarching plan: Section 9.4 of the National Development Programme 2030, "Accessible and Sustainable Health Care", sets six targets (85% health insurance coverage, life expectancy of 75 years, maternal mortality of 22, under-5 mortality of 14.0, a 30% reduction in premature NCD mortality, and 70% coverage of prevention and primary care) and five challenges.
paras.b: NDP 2030 9.4: six targets (85% insurance coverage, life expectancy 75, etc.)

paras.t: Core health plan: the Programme for the Protection of Public Health and Development of the Health Care System 2019–2030 ("Healthy Person – Prosperous Country") (Government Resolution No. 600 of 20 December 2018, amended in 2024 by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 802). It is the fourth health reform programme, following "Manas" (1996–2006), "Manas Taalimi" (2006–2010) and "Den Sooluk" (2012–2018). It aims to protect health, ensure access to necessary quality services, strengthen primary care and reduce financial hardship, with the goal of universal health coverage (UHC) by 2030.
paras.b: Health Programme 2019–2030: fourth health reform programme, targeting UHC

paras.t: Content (draft just before adoption): the World Bank's 2018 information document states that the programme sets 10 priority areas: four by level of care (public health, primary care, hospitals, emergency care) and six cross-cutting areas (laboratory services, medicines and medical devices, human resources, e-health, governance, financing). Its stated objective is "improving health outcomes and quality of services", with costs estimated at USD 1.47 billion.
paras.b: 10 priority areas (4 by level of care + 6 cross-cutting)

paras.t: Implementation: the programme runs in two phases, with an action plan for the first five years (2019–2023); the plan for the next phase was to build on first-phase results. It includes an indicator framework (baselines, interim and final targets) to be revised at a mid-term review after five years. As of September 2023, the Ministry of Health was preparing the 2024–2030 action plan.
paras.b: Two-phase implementation; 2024–2030 action plan in preparation (as of September 2023)

paras.t: The policy tree on this site groups the 10 areas into three pillars, following the World Bank technical assessment (2019): (1) primary care and public health, (2) hospitals and emergency care, and (3) health system foundations. Of the 10 areas, "public health and primary care" form Pillar 1, "hospitals and emergency care" Pillar 2, and the six cross-cutting areas Pillar 3.

Continued priorities: the WHO evaluation states that the programme carries over the priorities of the previous plan, "Den Sooluk" (cardiovascular disease, maternal and child health, TB, HIV), and aims for intersectoral collaboration and access to care for all, including vulnerable groups.

Monitoring: an annual Joint Annual Review (Ministry of Health and partners) is held. At its final meeting in October 2025, the Minister of Health named "NCD prevention" and "primary care development" as the two directions underpinning the health system.
paras.b: Joint Annual Review (October 2025): NCD prevention and primary care as the two directions

paras.t: Note: the programme text, its indicator framework, the 2024 amendment (Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 802) and the 2024–2030 action plan could not be found in a freely accessible source and have not been reviewed. Baselines and 2030 target values are therefore not stated.
Health financing arrangements and recent reforms

The national health insurance system is funded more than 70% from the state budget rather than contributions. The Mandatory Health Insurance Fund channels 80% of public spending through contracts with health facilities. The basic benefit (the State Guaranteed Benefits Package) is available to those registered with primary care, while additional coverage, including inpatient care and rehabilitation, applies to contributors and to people for whom the state pays contributions.

Under recent reforms, budget funds previously held by the Fund have been transferred to the Ministry of Health, and the Fund's regional branches are becoming regional departments of the Ministry. The Fund is expected to oversee quality and contracting; the report states that its role as a "strategic purchaser" is being undermined, and describes the impact on programme budgeting and performance indicators as "unclear".

Earlier reforms introduced case-based hospital payment in 2001–2004 and revised TB payment to favour outpatient treatment. In 2020, a pilot to regulate prices of the Additional Drug Package was conducted with WHO technical support.

The national target of 85% health insurance coverage will have to be pursued alongside reforms that shrink the Fund's role. Uncertainty over who manages insurance enrolment and payment appears to be one reason why no coverage rate is published.

In digital health, the primary care electronic database is used to monitor performance, and a mobile phone application maintained service delivery during COVID-19. Work is under way to use digital tools to strengthen the gatekeeping function and improve management of hypertension and diabetes.

sections.msg: Disease-specific programmes are concentrated in Pillar 1, while many areas in Pillars 2 and 3 have no stand-alone programme.

fig.cap: Table 1-1 Sub-programmes (active cooperation by matrix row; overlaps included)

paras.t: Pillar 1 (primary care and public health) contains plans for heart disease, kidney disease, mental health, immunization, TB, HIV and health emergencies. Pillar 2 (hospitals and emergency care) and Pillar 3 (health system foundations) include areas, such as emergency care, with no stand-alone programme.
paras.b: Disease plans concentrate in Pillar 1; few stand-alone plans in Pillars 2 and 3

paras.t: Of the six NDP 2030 targets, "85% health insurance coverage" and "70% primary care coverage" have neither a responsible sub-programme nor annually published data. This is the widest gap between targets and implementation.
paras.b: 85% insurance and 70% PHC coverage: no responsible plan, no published data

paras.t: In communicable diseases, plans are either drafts (HIV, health emergencies) or close to expiry (TB): national plans are not yet settled despite large donor funding.
paras.b: Communicable disease plans are drafts or near expiry, despite large funding

paras.t: Of the 14 plans and regulations in Table 1-1, 8 are in force, 3 are drafts (NCDs overall, HIV, health emergencies), 1 is nearing expiry (TB) and 2 have no stand-alone plan (maternal and child health, emergency care).

Plans in force are concentrated in disease-specific areas and in medicines and digital health; no plan covering health system foundations (workforce, primary care quality) appears in the table. These foundations are driven by the Health Programme 2019–2030 itself and the budget.

sections.msg: In 2026, institutional changes continued in NCDs, medicines and medical education.

fig.cap: From the quarterly report (Autumn 2026 edition). Updated each quarter

sections.h: Alignment with the WHO Country Cooperation Strategy 2024–2030
sections.msg: The WHO Country Cooperation Strategy has three strategic directions and seven priorities, many of them in areas with thin donor funding, such as hypertension, mental health, health emergencies and the health workforce.

fig.cap: Table 1-2 WHO's seven priorities × site matrix rows × active donor funding

paras.t: WHO and the Ministry of Health signed the Country Cooperation Strategy 2024–2030 in November 2023. It comprises three strategic directions and seven priority areas, and is aligned with the national health programme "Healthy Person – Prosperous Country".
paras.b: Signed November 2023; 3 directions and 7 priorities aligned with the national health programme

paras.t: The seven priority areas are: (1) hypertension; (2) health emergency prevention, preparedness and response; (3) mental health; (4) antimicrobial resistance (AMR); (5) climate resilience and chemical safety; (6) health workforce; and (7) data and digital health. The strategy also covers primary care and health financing, immunization, HIV and TB, and road safety.

2024 developments: a national NCD plan was adopted by the government on 12 April 2024. Three ministries signed the National Action Plan for Health Security 2024–2026 (12 areas). A health labour market analysis was conducted.
paras.b: 2024: national NCD plan adopted; health security action plan

paras.t: Of the seven priorities, mental health, the health workforce and health emergencies overlap with areas that the site's gap table shows as having little or no active donor funding. WHO technical support is the main entry point for filling these funding gaps.
paras.b: WHO priorities such as mental health and workforce overlap with thinly funded areas

paras.t: Note: the strategy document itself (a 70-page PDF) could not be opened; the priority areas were confirmed from the signing announcement and the table of contents of the annual report.

WHO's first priority, hypertension, is consistent with the Observatory's finding that high systolic blood pressure is the largest risk factor, associated with 21.9% of deaths. Yet active donor funding in the NCD row is only about USD 1.5 million, a large mismatch between priority and funding.

sections.h: Overview: outlook for the six national targets
sections.msg: Among targets trackable with annual data, premature NCD mortality is on track, life expectancy is off track, and maternal and child health depends on the data source.

fig.cap: Table 2-1 Gap to targets (actual pace = average annual change over the period; required pace = change needed to reach the target by 2030)

paras.t: Of the six NDP 2030 targets, four can be tracked with annual data: life expectancy, under-5 mortality, maternal mortality and premature NCD mortality. No published data were found for health insurance coverage or primary care coverage.
paras.b: Only 4 of the 6 targets can be tracked annually

paras.t: Life expectancy is rising by +0.19 years per year, against +0.43 years per year needed to reach 75 by 2030; at the current pace it will reach only about 73.5 years.
paras.b: Life expectancy: about 73.5 years in 2030 at current pace (target 75)

paras.t: Under-5 mortality is on track according to national statistics but off track according to UN estimates. The conclusion depends on which source is used.
paras.b: Under-5 mortality: on track in national data, off track in UN estimates

paras.t: The 2.6-year gap in life expectancy appears to be driven largely by high adult cardiovascular mortality. The age-standardized death rate from ischaemic heart disease was 390 per 100,000 (2016), about three times the WHO European Region's 120 (2019). Reaching the life expectancy target depends more on adult NCD control than on maternal and child health.

The fact that two of the six targets (health insurance coverage and primary care coverage) cannot be measured means that progress on the health system's foundations, financing and primary care, cannot be tracked against national targets. Disease indicators can be tracked; system indicators cannot.

The international target for premature NCD mortality (SDG 3.4.1) is a one-third reduction from 2015, equivalent to 16.8%. Reading the national target (a 30% reduction) against a 2015 baseline gives 17.6%; the 2023 value of 18.3% is still slightly short of both.

sections.h: Maternal and child health and nutrition
sections.msg: Child mortality continues to fall and antenatal care and facility births are near-universal; the remaining issues are post-discharge care and inconsistent statistics.

fig.cap: Figure 2-1 Under-5 mortality and maternal mortality (dotted lines = national and international targets)

paras.t: Trends: under-5 mortality fell from 17.8 (2020) to 16.8 (2024) in UN estimates, and from 17.9 (2021) to 15.9 (2024) in national statistics. Infant mortality fell from 14.4 (2020) to 13.1 (2024).
paras.b: Under-5 mortality 16.8 (UN) / 15.9 (national), both declining

paras.t: Services: 94% of women had four or more antenatal visits and facility births are close to 100% (MICS 2023). However, postnatal visits after discharge reach only 64% of mothers and 76% of newborns.
paras.b: Antenatal care 94%, facility births near 100%; postnatal visits only 64% of mothers

paras.t: Maternal mortality: the Ministry of Health figure is 25.7 (2024), close to the target of 22, but the UN estimate is 42 (2023), about twice the target. The WHO European Observatory reports 50.4 in 2020, against a Central Asian average of 24.3.
paras.b: Maternal mortality: MoH 25.7 vs UN estimate 42, a wide gap

paras.t: SDG benchmarks: under-5 mortality (SDG: 25 or below) and neonatal mortality (12 or below; 10.4 in MICS) already meet SDG levels. Maternal mortality also meets the SDG threshold of "below 70".

SDG levels have been met, and the national targets are set higher, aiming for "the top tier in Central Asia". Without an explanation of the gap between UN estimates and Ministry of Health figures (counting methods, under-reporting), assessments of achievement will remain unstable.
paras.b: SDGs already met; national target assessment hinges on data discrepancies

paras.t: Related cooperation: 12 projects worth about USD 33.5 million in the maternal and child health row (about USD 32.3 million from Germany). Most end in 2026 or 2027.
Background and drivers

In MICS 2023, only 34% of women had eight or more antenatal visits, and visits within one week after birth reached 56% of mothers and 65% of newborns. Antenatal visit frequency and postnatal care are not as widespread as facility births.

The UN estimate of maternal mortality rose from 58 (2015) to 70 (2021) and then fell to 42 (2023), rising during the COVID-19 years and then recovering; its level differs substantially from the Ministry of Health figures (37.1 in 2021, 25.7 in 2024).
In the household environment, access to safely managed drinking water is 67.3% in rural areas versus 90.8% in urban areas (2022), a gap that affects the health of rural mothers and children.

With facility births now near-universal, the remaining scope for improvement lies in the quality and frequency of antenatal care, post-discharge care and rural living conditions. Maternal and child health is entering a phase in which the focus shifts from hospitals to community-based primary care and home visits.

Related cooperation: of the 12 projects worth about USD 33.5 million in the maternal and child health row, Germany accounts for about USD 32.3 million, other bilateral donors for about USD 0.8 million and UNICEF for about USD 0.4 million.

Because the national target (maternal mortality of 22) is defined to be measured by Ministry of Health figures, national statistics show it as "nearly reached". Measured by the UN estimate (42), mortality is about twice the target, and the Observatory comparison (50.4 in 2020 against a Central Asian average of 24.3) also places it above average. Reports and consultations need to state explicitly which figure is being used each time.

sections.msg: Premature NCD mortality has fallen close to the national target; risk factors (tobacco, blood pressure) and disease-specific planning are the next stage.

fig.cap: Figure 2-2 Probability of dying from NCDs between ages 30 and 69

paras.t: Trends: the probability of dying between ages 30 and 69 from NCDs (cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease) fell from 25.2% (2015) to 18.3% (2023), up slightly from 17.7% in 2022.
paras.b: Premature NCD mortality 25.2% (2015) → 18.3% (2023)

paras.t: Risk factors: adult tobacco use is 22.2% (2024) and is not expected to meet the WHO 2025 target of 19.7%. Alcohol consumption is declining. The WHO European Observatory cites high blood pressure, diet, air pollution and smoking as the main risk factors.
paras.b: Smoking 22.2%, not expected to meet WHO 2025 target of 19.7%

paras.t: Cancer: about 8,900 new cases are diagnosed each year (2024 estimate), most commonly breast, stomach, lung, colorectal and cervical. The Minister of Health stated that the 2027 cancer care budget is 2.5 billion som against a requirement of 6 billion som.
paras.b: Cancer care budget: 2.5 billion som against 6 billion som needed (2027)

paras.t: Plans: national plans are in place for heart disease (2025–30) and kidney disease (2026–30), and an overall NCD strategy for 2027–2032 is in draft. There is no national cancer programme. The WHO Annual Report 2024 states that "a national NCD plan was adopted by the government on 12 April 2024", but which document this refers to has not been confirmed.

The national target of a "30% reduction" does not specify a baseline year. Against 2015 it is nearly achieved, but a later baseline would put it further away. The target definition needs to be confirmed first.
paras.b: The "30% reduction" target has no stated baseline year

paras.t: Related cooperation: about USD 1.5 million is active (a Swiss project nearing completion, and WHO). Cooperation completed since 2017 totals about USD 10.6 million.
paras.b: Active NCD cooperation is only about USD 1.5 million

paras.t: Donor funding is among the lowest for the area that accounts for most deaths.
Risk factors and primary care

According to the Observatory, the risk factors associated with all deaths in 2021 were high systolic blood pressure 21.9%, diet 18.1%, tobacco 14.1%, high body mass index (BMI) 13.7% and air pollution 9.4%. The age-standardized death rate from ischaemic heart disease was 390 per 100,000 (2016), about three times the European Region's 120.

Smoking exceeds 50% among men, and 25.5% of boys and 8.9% of girls aged 13–15 have tried tobacco. Tobacco taxes are among the lowest in the European Region, and smoking cessation medicines are not covered by the state benefit package. Adult overweight rose from 38.3% (2000) to 48.3% (2016), and obesity from 9.6% to 16.6%.

In international data series, adult tobacco use fell from 28.1% (2010) to 22.2% (2024), per capita alcohol consumption from 4.14 L (2019) to 3.29 L (2023), while diabetes prevalence (ages 20–79) rose from 6.3% (2011) to 7.6% (2024).

On primary care, the report notes that patients often bypass primary care and go directly to hospitals, that the gatekeeping role is weak, and that NCD and prevention efforts are insufficient. Efforts are under way to use digital tools to manage hypertension and diabetes.

Premature mortality has fallen, but the risk factors of blood pressure, obesity and smoking remain high or are increasing. Whether current gains are sustained depends on primary care's capacity to detect hypertension and keep patients on treatment; fiscal instruments such as higher tobacco taxes are not being used.

Related cooperation: the NCD row has 6 active projects worth about USD 1.5 million, with Switzerland at about USD 1.2 million and WHO at about USD 0.3 million. Cooperation completed since 2017 comprises 30 projects worth about USD 10.6 million.
Alcohol consumption is 4 L per capita (2019), below the European Region's 7.8 L. Among risk factors, blood pressure, diet, tobacco and obesity weigh more heavily than alcohol.

Comparing the weight of risk factors with funding and plans, heart disease (Presidential Decree) and kidney disease plans are now in place, but areas requiring policies outside the Ministry of Health, such as tobacco taxation, diet and obesity, are barely visible in either national plans or donor projects.

sections.msg: Immunization has recovered, but TB and HIV are furthest from international targets and remain largely donor-funded.

fig.cap: Figure 2-3 New TB cases and measles vaccination coverage

paras.t: TB: new cases fell from 178 per 100,000 (2015) to 131 (2020), then stayed almost flat at 128 (2024). This is the indicator furthest from the WHO targets (89 by 2025, 36 by 2030). Kyrgyzstan is one of the 30 high-burden countries for multidrug-resistant TB, with a treatment success rate for MDR-TB of 55%.
paras.b: TB 128 (2024): furthest from the WHO 2025 target of 89

paras.t: HIV: about 13,000 people are living with HIV, of whom 6,900 are on treatment (2024). The state now covers 90% of treatment costs (60% in 2021).
paras.b: HIV: 6,900 of about 13,000 on treatment; state covers 90%

paras.t: Immunization: measles coverage of 96% (2024) meets the WHO 95% benchmark, but DTP3 fell from 95% (2019) to 87% (2020) and recovered only to 90% (2022).
paras.b: Measles 96%; DTP3 at 90%, not fully recovered

paras.t: Global Fund grants are the backbone of TB and HIV funding, and the current grant period ends at the end of 2026 (USD 27 million for 2024–2026, UNAIDS). The state's share is rising, but the scale of successor funding will determine outcomes.
paras.b: Global Fund grant period ends at the end of 2026

paras.t: Related cooperation: about USD 40.7 million in the HIV and hepatitis row, about USD 49.5 million in immunization (mainly Gavi) and about USD 7.7 million in TB (United States).
Background and drivers

TB treatment success rates are 81% for drug-susceptible TB (2018 cohort; regional average 75%) and 55% for MDR-TB (regional average 59%). The share of cases detected and treated fell from 78.3% (2008) to 71.3% (2017). Introduction of all-oral regimens and video-observed treatment is planned.

The CDC reports a TB treatment success rate of 86% for 2024. HIV has not reached the UNAIDS 2025 "95-95-95" targets (shares of people who know their status, receive treatment and achieve viral suppression).
In immunization, DTP3 fell from 95% (2019) to 87% (2020) and has recovered only to 90% (2022). Measles coverage recovered: 99% (2015), 92% (2020) and 96% (2024).

The flat trend in new TB cases since 2020 needs to be read alongside the declining share of cases detected and linked to treatment. Weak case detection means the numbers either fail to fall or fall only on paper.

Related cooperation: immunization row, 11 projects worth about USD 49.5 million (Gavi/Global Fund about USD 44 million, UNICEF about USD 4.6 million, WHO about USD 1 million); HIV and hepatitis row, 10 projects worth about USD 40.7 million (Global Fund about USD 24.2 million, UNDP about USD 14 million, United States about USD 2.6 million); TB row, 2 projects worth about USD 7.7 million (United States); health emergencies row, 16 projects worth about USD 17.7 million (ADB about USD 15 million).

The TB row has about USD 158 million in cooperation completed since 2017, but only about USD 7.7 million active. Even allowing for Global Fund TB/HIV grants also being counted in the HIV row, external funding for TB has fallen sharply.
About 13,000 people are living with HIV (2024 estimate); the 6,900 on treatment represent about 53%. Even on the second "95" (share receiving treatment) alone, the gap to the target is large.

The state's share of HIV treatment costs rose from 60% (2021) to 90%, moving antiretroviral medicines close to full funding from the state budget. Remaining dependence on external funding appears to lie in prevention, testing and outreach to key populations. The end of the Global Fund grant period will hit this area hardest.

sections.msg: Out-of-pocket spending is at 40% and rising again, and the health insurance target (85% coverage) has no data to measure it.

fig.cap: Figure 2-4 Out-of-pocket share of health spending and UHC service coverage index

paras.t: Out-of-pocket spending: fell from 56.3% (2014) to 39.1% (2021), then rose to 42.3% (2023). The WHO benchmark is 20% or less.
paras.b: OOP 39.1% (2021) → 42.3% (2023); benchmark 20% or less

paras.t: Coverage: about one-third of the population cannot make full use of the State Guaranteed Benefits Package and the Additional Drug Package. Outpatient medicines are limited to about 70 items with a 50% price subsidy. Some of the Health Insurance Fund's functions are set to move to the Ministry of Health.
paras.b: Outpatient medicines limited to about 70 items with 50% subsidy

paras.t: The UHC service coverage index stands at 74 and has been flat since 2015.
paras.b: UHC service coverage index flat at 74

paras.t: Spending on primary care is about 1% of GDP, and public primary care spending per capita is among the lowest in the WHO European Region.
Workforce: the numbers of physicians and nurses are among the lowest in the European Region, and ageing and emigration continue.
NDP 2030 targets "85% health insurance coverage", but no annual coverage figures could be found, so progress cannot be measured. Building the measurement system is itself an opportunity for support.
paras.b: Building a system to measure insurance coverage is itself a support opportunity

paras.t: Related cooperation: about USD 23.4 million in the financing and UHC row (almost entirely Germany's sector support, ending in December 2026). Workforce and medical education: about USD 1.2 million.
Background and drivers

According to the Observatory, 46% of households reported difficulty paying for health care in 2014, up from 38% in 2009. The main drivers of catastrophic spending are outpatient medicines and outpatient and inpatient care, and out-of-pocket costs are the main reason people go without medicines. Out-of-pocket payments for inpatient care are also widespread.

Health's share of government expenditure fell from 14.5% (2006) to 6.9% (2020), then recovered to 8.6% (2021). Hospital beds per 100,000 fell from 1,206 (1991) to 697 (2000) and 422 (2021), but the report still considers this too many relative to income and the young population.

Expanding coverage of medicines, which account for 30% of health spending, appears the most effective way to reduce out-of-pocket spending. This would require bringing health's share of government expenditure closer to its 2006 level, or reducing hospital beds and redirecting the savings to primary care and medicines.

Related cooperation: primary care model row, 9 projects worth about USD 29 million (World Bank about USD 27.3 million); financing and UHC row, 6 projects worth about USD 23.4 million (Germany about USD 22.5 million, Switzerland about USD 1 million); workforce and medical education, 8 projects worth about USD 1.2 million; digital health, 3 projects worth about USD 0.3 million. The medicines and medical devices row has no active projects.

Under the Additional Drug Package, the state pays 50% of the "base price" of listed medicines and patients pay the difference from the retail price. The Observatory notes that the lack of clarity over the scope of public coverage, for both patients and providers, is increasing the burden.

The UHC service coverage index remaining at 74 for eight years is consistent with service coverage not expanding while out-of-pocket payments continue to fill the gap. Together with the inability to measure insurance coverage, this means indicators of UHC progress have stalled on both national targets and international indicators.

In terms of workforce composition, 64.9% of physicians are women (2019), and family doctors account for only 12% of physicians (2021). There are about 3,000 vacant primary care physician posts, and more than half of family doctors are at retirement age. If only 30% of young doctors continue to enter the public system, vacancies will grow further.

paras.t: Allocation by area and the outlook from 2027

By matrix row, active funding is largest in immunization (about USD 49.5 million), followed by HIV and hepatitis (about USD 40.7 million), maternal and child health (about USD 33.5 million), hospital restructuring and modernization (about USD 31.3 million), primary care model (about USD 29 million), financing and UHC (about USD 23.4 million), health emergencies (about USD 17.7 million) and TB (about USD 7.7 million).
paras.tnj: By matrix row, active funding is largest in immunization (about USD 49.5 million), followed by HIV and hepatitis (about USD 40.7 million), maternal and child health (about USD 33.5 million), primary care model (about USD 29 million), financing and UHC (about USD 23.4 million), health emergencies (about USD 17.7 million) and TB (about USD 7.7 million).

paras.t: The about USD 72.2 million ending at the end of 2026 breaks down as Germany about USD 40.1 million, Global Fund about USD 24.2 million, UNDP about USD 6.5 million and Switzerland about USD 1.3 million.

Excluding projects ending in late 2026, active funding falls to about USD 167 million. Germany drops from about USD 54.7 million to about USD 14.6 million and Gavi/Global Fund from about USD 68.1 million to about USD 43.9 million (mainly immunization), leaving financing and UHC and HIV particularly thinly funded.

Funding concentrates in areas where results are easy to count, such as immunization, HIV and maternal and child health, while system areas such as the workforce, primary care quality and medicines receive little. Funding allocation does not match the largest challenges: out-of-pocket spending and the workforce.

The medicines area has had 14 projects in the past but none is active. Given that medicines account for 30% of health spending and are a main driver of out-of-pocket costs, this is a significant gap.

The health emergencies row has about USD 57.6 million in cooperation completed since 2017 (including the COVID-19 response) and about USD 17.7 million active. Emergency funding has declined since COVID-19, but ADB projects are supporting preparedness.

sections.msg: Four areas have no active cooperation: primary care quality, primary care workforce, emergency care and medicines.

fig.cap: Table 3-3 Strategy areas × donors (toggle between active, completed and cumulative)

paras.t: Areas with no active cooperation: primary care quality, primary care workforce, emergency care and medicines.
paras.b: Gaps: PHC quality and workforce, emergency care, medicines

paras.t: Of these four gaps, three (primary care quality, primary care workforce and emergency care) also have no cooperation completed since 2017. Medicines has 14 completed projects worth about USD 2.1 million.

The primary care workforce gap coincides with more than half of family doctors being at retirement age and only 30% of young doctors entering the public system. This appears to be the area with the widest mismatch between the funding gap and the size of the challenge.

Emergency care has no stand-alone national plan (Table 1-1) and no active or completed cooperation. It is the only area in the health matrix where both plans and funding are absent, and it needs to start with building the institutional framework.

sections.msg: 2027 will test both donor successor funding and the formal adoption of national plans at the same time.

paras.t: Large cooperation programmes for HIV and TB (Global Fund) and for financing and maternal and child health (Germany) end in late 2026, and the scale of their successors will directly affect communicable disease and out-of-pocket indicators.
paras.b: Successors to large programmes will drive communicable disease and OOP indicators

paras.t: Three national plans, for HIV and hepatitis, health emergencies and NCDs, are still in draft; whether they are formally adopted will be the entry point for donors' next round of support.
paras.b: Formal adoption of HIV, health emergency and NCD plans is the entry point for support

paras.t: The gap areas (primary care quality and workforce, emergency care, medicines) are being addressed through the national budget, presidential decrees and components of other projects. Here, technical cooperation on institution-building is likely to be in greater demand than funding.
paras.b: Gap areas are likely to call for technical cooperation on institution-building

paras.t: Reaching the life expectancy target depends on adult NCDs, especially hypertension control, yet NCDs and the primary care workforce receive the least funding. In planning successor funding, the question is whether the centre of gravity can shift from disease-specific areas to primary care foundations.

On indicators, building systems to measure the two targets of health insurance coverage and primary care coverage is the first requirement, regardless of funding levels. Targets that cannot be measured make it hard for donors to demonstrate results and are unlikely to become entry points for support.
